newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish court bars government papers from EU trial.
newsitem.headline: Danish court bars government papers from EU trial.

text.p: A Danish court setting rules for a legal battle over Danish soveriegnty and the EU gave the first round to the government on Tuesday when it said that confidential cabinet papers could not be brought in evidence.
Replying to a request by 11 citizens seeking to prove that transfer of national powers to the EU contravenes the Danish constitution, the court said that the papers were irrelevant.
"Submission of the documents cannot be considered to have any bearing on the court's judgment of the appellants' claim," the written verdict said.

Christian Harlang, a lawyer for the non-partisan group of 11, said that they would appeal the decision, which is part of procedural hearings ahead of the main trial, expected to open next year at the earliest.

"We will go to the Supreme Court so there's no reason either to cheer or weep," he told Reuters adding that even if he failed to win an appeal on the question of evidence, the case itself was still winnable.
"Even without these documents our chances of winning the case are still good," he said.
He thought the appeal would be heard within three weeks.

The challengers seek to prove their case by examining documents dating back to Denmark's 1973 membership of the EU and beyond, while the government wants debate confined to events subsequent to the 1992 Maastricht accord.
Lawyers say that whoever wins this opening procedural stage will have an advantage when the case begins in earnest.

Ultimately at stake in the case, expected to last at least two years, is whether Denmark can carry on as a member of the EU under existing terms, or must choose between renegotiating membership and attempting to amend the constitution.
Danes have a history of coolness toward the EU.

They rejected Maastricht altogether in a 1992 referendum and approved it the following year only on condition that Denmark stay out of European Monetary Union and joint defence, policing and citizenship arrangements.
